newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Congress passes changes in OPA '90 Act.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Congress passes changes in OPA '90 Act.

text.p: The U.S. Congress in weekend action voted to keep the certificate of financial responsibility requirement for offshore facilities $35 million, but give the administration authority to require up to $150 million if there is higher risk oil spills.

The bill, sought by the oil industry and backed by the Clinton administration, would ease the blanket requirement that facilities demonstrate $150 million in financial responsibility -- a level the industry said would bar offshore operations to all but the largest companies.
The changes to the Oil Pollution Act of 1990 were passed as part of the Coast Guard authorization bill.
The bill requires a $10 million certificate of financial responsibility for operations in state waters.
It also generally exempts OPA '90 provisions from facilities that handle less than 1,000 barrels of oil at a time, although there can be exceptions.

The bill also had a number of measures intended to strengthen protections against oil spills, including requiring single-hulled oil-carrying barges to have means to prevent grounding, and requiring that all vessels that tow oil-carrying barges have fire-suppression measures.

It also clarifies oil spill response procedures, sets up a national clearinghouse of information on environmental effects of spills, and allows those who sustain economic loss from a spill to receive payments for short-term damages without losing their right to recover more damages later.

"The key thing to remember is the $150 million in the way the original law was written was unable to be implemented. This change had to been made," said Roy Willis, vice president of government relations with the Independent Petroleum Association of America.
"This removes the cloud of economic ruin from the independents who are moving into the offshore in a big way," Willis said.
